reviews.reason: With only elementary embeddings and finite induction allowed, the task must overcome a concrete failure of free amalgamation: a common pair can have different products on the two sides. The solution identifies those products while preserving induced embeddings and strongness, accounts for a loss of at most one bounded-strongness unit per identification, and then proves the asymmetric conclusions C strong and B n-strong using two different HF-order splicings. This controlled finite construction and quantitative uniform budget support H2. The result does not need H3 or any infinite saturated-model homogeneity claim.
reviews.core_assessment: Read the complete main proof742-749 and all local support before selector rationale. A conflicting product b can be moved immediately after the old base in an HF-order: if moving it earlier created an additional lower block at an intervening point, that same block would have been a second lower pair for b before the move. The bounded version applies this argument to each base+b+X of total new size at most the old budget. At each identification the common induced structure remains the same because in both sides the newly common point can have only its one forced block with two old-base points; the available budget is at least1 whenever an identification is needed. Each step increases the intersection and eliminates one B-outside-base point, hence there are at most |B minus A| steps, leaving at least n units. At termination a doubled common pair cannot have two external products; triples with a product already in the common induced part cannot conflict either. Thus the free union is a partial STS. Placing C first and the remaining B points after it gives an HF-order; for an arbitrary X of size<=n on the C side, placing all B first followed by its original X-order works because no cross blocks exist outside the intersection. The n=0 case is also valid: the budget can reach zero only after all B-outside-base points have been identified, when the conclusion is immediate.
reviews.prerequisite_assessment: No amalgamation theorem, generic-model theorem or infinite saturation theorem is assumed. The finite HF-order criterion is elementary removal induction and is printed in the second author source. Its converse uses restriction of an HF-order to a subset and its greatest point. The additional propositional compactness paragraph is not used in this finite counted construction.

issues.decision: The sentence about the greatest a of A-prime incorrectly says at most one block of A before concluding at most one block of A-prime. The HF definition directly limits blocks whose other two points are below a; all points in A-prime other than a are below it, so the correct and needed conclusion is at most one block inside A-prime. Preserve the printed text and disclose this overbroad intermediate wording; the source definition and target subset uniquely determine the restriction.

The infinite compactness display omits a!=b in strict-order totality and would otherwise contradict irreflexivity. This is already disclosed in the task; the main author source780 prints the restricted totality correctly. The finite amalgamation uses only the preceding finite induction and does not rely on that defective displayed infinite theory.

core_obligations: Before forming a free union, identify the two possible products of every shared pair that occur on opposite sides, so the union still satisfies the partial-Steiner uniqueness axiom.
After every identification preserve strongness of the smaller side and decrease the finite strongness budget by at most1; show at most |B minus A| such identifications are needed.
Construct an HF-order with C first on the resulting free amalgam, proving it is unconfined and C remains strong.
For each set X of at most n new C-points, splice the two available HF-orders to prove the embedded B-copy is n-strong.

proof_roadmap.step: A forced product may be moved immediately above the base; adding it consumes at most one unit of n-strongness.
Iteratively identify conflicting products and account for the budget m=n+|B minus A|.
Place C first and then the remaining B-copy, producing an HF-order of the free amalgam.
For any at-most-n set X on the C-side, use the residual strongness and absence of cross blocks to put the B-copy first.

approved_task_config.difficulty_reason: Ordinary free union need not even be a partial Steiner system because a common pair can acquire two products. The proof designs a controlled identification process while tracking two distinct strengths of embedding, then constructs compatible HF-orders in both directions. The explicit uniform loss m=n+|B minus A| requires accounting for forced identifications and arbitrary bounded test sets; it is not an invocation of a standard amalgamation theorem.

editorial_notes: C_un is the class of finite unconfined partial Steiner triple systems (source437-440). The whole counted task has finite structures; n-strongness is the bounded test-set condition686-692.
The original author construction and proof are retained. The relation A<=B is strong-substructure order, not the HF linear order itself.

The external support proposition is by the same two authors in Endomorphisms of free Steiner quasigroups, fixed version2412.06055v3. Its finite induction supplies the criterion needed here; the printed infinite compactness clause includes a noted a!=b omission, but the counted finite construction does not use that clause.

In the support source line293, the greatest point of a finite subset A-prime is said to belong to at most one block of A. The needed and directly justified assertion is at most one block inside A-prime: the other two points of each such block lie below that greatest point in the HF-order. The printed broader intermediate wording is retained; the subset restriction follows from the source definition and is the conclusion used here.
